content:
TL;DR
Take on the cognitive load: edit and shorten AI drafts. Be clear about AI’s role when it affects how people should read the work. Check facts and sources before sharing them. Ask before using someone else’s work with an AI tool. Use AI when it helps; write it yourself when it doesn’t. Did AI save time for the team, or only for me? Generative AI makes it easy to produce messages, documents and presentations. But saving time for the person writing them does not always save time for the team. Sometimes using AI saves the writer ten minutes and costs everyone else twenty minutes trying to make sense of the result.
One phrase from a recent conversation with my colleagues stayed with me:
“Cognitive load shouldn’t shift from the writer to the reader.”
I have nothing against people using ChatGPT or Claude. What gets to me is opening a polished document, reading the headings and takeaways, and still having to work out what the author is actually saying. I’ve had that happen more than once.
When AI saves time for one person In 2025, BetterUp and Stanford Social Media Lab published research on “workslop”: AI-generated work that looks finished but creates more work for the person receiving it. In their survey, 53% of employees said at least some of the AI-generated work they send could probably fit that description.
That number didn’t surprise me. It is so easy now to produce another page, another set of options, another summary or table. Writing 1,500 words instead of 300 takes very little extra effort. We haven’t suddenly gained more time to read it all; somebody still has to work out what matters and what needs a response.
We have AI policies. Do we need AI etiquette as well? Our policies cover confidential information, personal data, security, intellectual property and customer communication. I started wondering what guidance we have for the everyday cases.
I mean the smaller things: a huge document that could have been five paragraphs, a statistic nobody checked, or a polished message that leaves you guessing what its author thinks.
While reading about this, I came across AITiquette, a community project about thoughtful AI use at work. I used AI to help with some of that research, which felt fitting. It got me thinking about the principles I want to follow, and I wrote down five.
1. Take on the cognitive load yourself If an AI assistant gives me 1,500 words, my colleague does not have to receive all 1,500. I still have to work out what’s worth sending and what they actually need.
I suggested to colleagues that we do more than proofread an AI draft: we should cut it down too. Some felt that was too much to ask for every little message. I can see their point. I still think that if AI saves me twenty minutes, I can spend a couple of those minutes making the message less of a chore for the next person.
Generating another page costs me almost nothing, but someone else still has to read it.
2. Be clear about where the work came from I do not think every Slack message needs an “AI-assisted” label. If I tagged every sentence an AI tool helped me rewrite, people would stop paying attention to the label. There are cases where the process matters, though. Did you analyse the data or ask a tool to summarise it? Did you read the original document? Did you check the recommendation? Are these your conclusions, or options a model came up with?
If I have only asked a model for options, I should say so. If I checked the source and read the original, I can say that too. My colleagues do not need a label on every message; they need enough context to know what I did and how much confidence to place in the result.
3. Don’t outsource fact-checking to the reader I’ve seen a confident “research shows” followed by a statistic and a link. Then I open the source and find it says something else. AI can help find research or navigate a long report, but I shouldn’t leave it to a colleague to check whether the claim holds up.
If I send someone a statistic, I should make sure the source exists, the number is right and it supports my point. A wrong claim can end up in a presentation or influence a decision before anyone catches it.
4. Be careful with other people’s work The answer depends on the context and the tools your company allows. Is it okay to upload someone else’s draft, summarise a private meeting, or rewrite a colleague’s text without telling them? What about using an internal discussion to generate a presentation?
Policies cover some of this, especially security and confidentiality. When I’m unsure about the everyday cases, I ask myself, “Would I be comfortable telling the person exactly what I did with their work?”
If not, I should ask first.
5. Use AI when it actually helps I use AI regularly. It helps me explore alternatives, challenge an argument, organise messy thoughts and handle repetitive work. But sometimes I reach for it just because it is there.
For example, I’ll ask a model to draft a short message, then delete the intro, the bullets and the conclusion until only four lines remain. I could probably have written those four lines myself.
I do not want to use AI just to say I used it. If I can’t point to what it improved, I probably didn’t need it.
A few habits may be enough When I brought these ideas to my colleagues, they had their own suggestions, and not everyone agreed with mine. That was helpful. More than once, someone asked me not to turn this into another internal document.
I understand why. Nobody wants another long policy to read. I’d rather see people read what they send, cut what their colleagues do not need, check their sources and say when they used AI if it matters. That seems like a good place to start.
My colleagues and I are still figuring out what good AI-assisted work looks like. I have started asking myself:
Did AI save time for the team, or only for me?
If the answer is “just me,” I know I have another edit to make before I send it.
I wrote the first draft of this article myself, then used AI to help revise and shorten it. I reviewed the final version and decided what to keep.
summary:
TL;DR

  1. Take on the cognitive load: edit and shorten AI drafts.
  2. Be clear about AI’s role when it affects how people should read the work.
  3. Check facts and sources before sharing them.
  4. Ask before using someone else’s work with an AI tool.
  5. Use AI when it helps; write it yourself when it doesn’t.

Did AI save time for the team, or only for me?

Generative AI makes it easy to produce messages, documents and presentations. But saving time for the person writing them does not always save time for the team. Sometimes using AI saves the writer ten minutes and costs everyone else twenty minutes trying to make sense of the result.

Salute! 👋 My name is Denis. I am an Engineering Manager with a backend background in Python and Go. I love doing optimizations: diving deep into a problem and looking for solutions.
I am very interested in high-load distributed systems. I believe that a long-living project requires good test coverage and possibly ugly but strict code style. And MVP is MVP.
These days I spend as much time on the team as on the code: building development processes, people management, goal setting and keeping engineers motivated. I share that experience here alongside the technical writing.
Love open source and studying programming languages development.
I am self-taught and have no computer science education, but before entering IT, I had some entrepreneurial and leadership experience, so I am well aware of how to prioritize business requirements and a technical debt.
Experience Engineering Manager, Safety team – inDrive, Tbilisi / Remote (November 2025 – present)
I lead a team of Android, iOS, backend and QA engineers distributed across 4 countries. We build worldwide distributed systems in Kotlin, Swift and Go that make inDrive a safer place for our customers.
Management Distributed systems Go Kotlin Swift
Senior backend engineer, acting as Tech Lead – Avito, Tbilisi / Remote (March 2024 – November 2025)
Anti-fraud team at Avito, the world’s largest online classifieds platform. I developed architecture and platform solutions, launched new services and improved system performance, while leading the team and managing processes.
Clustering & multi-account services. Designed and implemented a scalable clustering architecture with sharding and data migration: resource usage dropped ~2.5x (630 GB Redis → 250 GB MongoDB + 12 GB KeyDB), with better stability and SLO compliance. Designed and launched the multi-account management MVP, decomposed the work and led the team to a fast production release. Platform improvements. Implemented a shared caching library; extended other libraries with deadline propagation, context logging and assorted optimizations. Reliability & performance. Optimized Python services, introduced caching and data compression, removed bottlenecks and ran load testing to verify behaviour under high load. Delivery management. Formalized technical project workflows, maintained roadmaps and Jira dashboards — the team completed 90%+ of planned tasks. Team growth. Mentored developers, conducted interviews, improved the system design evaluation process and acted as feature lead on key initiatives. Community. Relaunched the internal Python community and organized meetups, increasing engineer engagement by 175%. Incidents & technical debt. Systematized incident and bug review, slowing the accumulation of technical debt. Python Go Distributed systems MongoDB Redis KeyDB Kafka Pulsar Kubernetes
Backend team lead – ITASystems (1CUPIS project), Moscow / Remote (February 2023 – March 2024)
1CUPIS is the only payment system for Russian legal bookmakers. I led a team of 10 people — developers, QA engineers and a system analyst — building the anti-fraud system and several related services.
made anti-fraud one of the best performing nodes of the whole payment system, improving its performance by 7x despite constantly growing business logic introduced approaches that help the team safely deliver features to a distributed system, reducing unsuccessful releases to a minimum arranged sharing of competencies through internal technical discussions, reducing the bus factor streamlined and systematised how the team maintains technical documentation Alongside that: team assessment and metrics, 1:1s and feedback, architectural solutions and contract negotiation, hiring and interviewing, planning and estimation, development and CI/CD process improvements, code review — and coding (when it’s possible 😀).
Management Kanban Python Django Flask PostgreSQL MongoDB Kafka RabbitMQ Docker Kubernetes
Software engineer – ITASystems (1CUPIS project), Moscow (June 2021 – January 2023)
I was responsible for the anti-fraud system, every service in its infrastructure, and for automating the business unit’s operations.
improved the services’ performance and stability by several times set up monitoring and alerting that lets the team spot and address issues early integrated the system with incident control and government services, which significantly reduced manual work for colleagues Optimization Python Django Flask PostgreSQL MongoDB Kafka RabbitMQ Docker Kubernetes Jaeger Kibana
Software engineer – Printum, Moscow (December 2020 – June 2021)
I developed backend and frontend for SaaS, an embedded product, and a small mobile application.
Of the non-trivial things I had to do:
an integration with ActiveDirectory (users sync) an embedded application for Xerox MFPs Since the team was small, I took on some more unusual functions, such as:
working with customers: deploying embedded software in their infrastructure, preparing for a presentation, consulting administrators working with outsourcing teams product delivery automation: packaging, uploading to S3, installation from S3 to the customer’s local network publishing of a mobile application to Google Play and AppStore. Python Django DRF PostgreSQL Docker Nginx Vue.js jQuery LDAP SNMP Ansible Bash
Test automation engineer – Tensor, Novosibirsk (December 2019 – November 2020)
I was engaged in the automation of UI and API testing of the warehouse accounting system.
In addition to the tests themselves, I developed elements of the company’s testing framework, and also set up CI in Jenkins: built pipelines for various types of tests (smoke, acceptance, integration), wrote Groovy scripts to update the test environment.
Python Selenium Jenkins Groovy Docker Linux Page object
Junior Python developer – E-commerce, self-employed, Novosibirsk (June 2018 – November 2019)
I built a back-office system for my own e-commerce business with Python, Flask and PostgreSQL.
automated price list collection from suppliers’ websites integrated with external marketplaces (Drom.ru, Auto.ru) implemented tools to find optimal prices across overlapping items I also ran the business end to end: supplier relations, marketing, SEO, customer service, sales, logistics and accounting. This is what led me to IT.
Python Flask PostgreSQL Problem solving Liquid InSales Yandex Direct

Commanded a company and organized machines operation in conditions of persistent multiprocessing.
Management Planning Multitasking
